title: Final Project: Monte Carlo Study
text:
The final project is to implement a complete Monte Carlo study.
Base the study on either your own research project or a paper of your choice.

A well-cited, relatively recent paper is sufficient.
A paper with publicly available replication code is even better.
Let me know if you have difficulty finding a suitable paper.

Please briefly describe your plan in a GitHub issue and assign the issue to me.
The final project is due on August 23 at 23:59.
Submit a PDF typeset in LaTeX and the accompanying Julia code.
The required contents are provided below.

I know the exact structure may vary with your setting. But the point is it’s important to show the intermediate outputs for validation, not just showing that you recover true parameters.

title: Final Project: Monte Carlo Study
text:
Required Contents

Goal

Briefly state the goal of your Monte Carlo study. It does not need to be detailed.
For example, “I want to implement this method correctly” or “I want to conduct this counterfactual experiment” is sufficient.



Setting and Data-Generating Process

Describe the setting and data-generating process (DGP) in enough detail for readers who are unfamiliar with the paper.



Identification

Report the point- or set-identified parameter values implied by the identification conditions.
If the parameter is point identified, the recovered value should be within 1% of the true value.
If the parameter is set identified, a visual presentation of the identified set is preferred.
You may omit this section if identification analysis does not apply to your setting.



Summary Statistics

Report summary statistics for the simulated datasets.



Estimation

Show how the objective function behaves near the true parameter values.
Report the estimates. Their mean should be within 5% of the true value.
Inference is optional, but I encourage you to try it.



Counterfactual Analysis

Consider one or two interesting counterfactual scenarios and summarize their implications.
Inference for the counterfactual results is optional.

title: Julia for Empirical Economics
text: Hi! Thank you for your interest in this class! I am very excited to offer this new module, because I could not find, at least online, a class designed around the core idea that LLMs can be used extensively to conduct structural estimation in Julia. I hope this module will be useful for your own research. I look forward to meeting you in class.

title: Julia for Empirical Economics
text:
Instructor
Instructor: Kosuke Shimamoto, kosuke.shimamoto@duke.edu

title: Julia for Empirical Economics
text:
Course Principle

This module is designed to help students independently develop and implement their own empirical economics projects entirely in Julia.
This module is based on the idea that the most effective way to learn a programming language is to implement things yourself, even if you use extensive support from LLMs.
The lectures aim to give students a high-level understanding of how to use Julia and related computational techniques.

I will move relatively quickly to introduce the main ideas across many topics.

I will not cover every detail of the programming language in lecture.
This is because you can use LLMs to study many implementation details on your own.

To complement the lectures, this module assigns many hands-on exercises.
This module strongly encourages the use of LLMs. But of course, you remain responsible for their outputs.

title: Julia for Empirical Economics
text:
Class Style

Given the course principles, each class consists of a lecture and in-class activities.
The lecture portion will take about 90 minutes, and the remaining 55 minutes will be for in-class activities. You can ask the instructor any questions during the latter half of the class.
If you have finished the in-class activity for the day, you can work on the assignments, the final project, or your own work. The goal is to let you use class time productively.

title: Julia for Empirical Economics
text:
Grading and Assignments
Your course grade will depend on three components:

In-class assignments (30%): There will be one in-class assignment for each class. You need to submit it within 24 hours after the class ends. The grade is on a binary scale and is evaluated by effort. If you write at least one line of code, you will receive full credit. You receive full credit for this component if you correctly submit 7 of the 9 assignments, so you may miss 2 assignments.
Three coding homework assignments (40%): You will be assigned weekly assignments during this class. The grades are evaluated by correctness. Each student must submit their own answer. All assignments are equally weighted.
Final project (30%): You will be asked to complete a Monte Carlo simulation as the final project. The final project should be based on 1) your own work, 2) a paper you like, or 3) papers I suggest. More details are documented in a separate file.


Due

HW1: Jul 26, 23:59
HW2: Aug 2, 23:59
HW3: Aug 9, 23:59
Final Project: Aug 23, 23:59

Requirements

All code must be written in Julia. You may call other languages from Julia if necessary.
You must submit your code and its outputs.
You can submit outputs in any format, such as PDF, HTML, or Word, except for the final project. The final project should be submitted as a PDF typeset in LaTeX because this is the format commonly expected for our research.
I recommend submitting homework as HTML files compiled from Quarto, because Quarto integrates well with Julia and is easy to write in.
Before I introduce Git and GitHub, you will submit assignments via Canvas. After we learn GitHub, you must submit them via GitHub.
